solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable copy, its numbering matching the numbers printed in it and the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What to take exercise in? Notes will include pang when running

indicators.note: running here means in disorder, like a mixture that runs, so the letters are rearranged
to include something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: jots are brief written notes
the letters of pang, mixed

explanation.surface: A jogger's resolution: keep notes on the pain felt while out running.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by description rather than synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Jogpants are loose trousers worn for running and other exercise, so they are what you exercise in.

clue.text: Servant with boiling teapot near — one gets baked (12, two words)

indicators.note: boiling water churns about, so the following word's letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: a jack is a manservant or general labourer
teapot rearranged
to can mean close against, as in cheek to cheek

explanation.surface: A servant stands by a boiling teapot, while something else bakes.
explanation.walkthrough: TO for near is a stretch: it is the sense in 'cheek to cheek' or 'push the door to'.
explanation.definitionFit: A jacket potato is a potato baked whole in its skin, so it is one item that gets baked.

clue.text: Old woman's taken over shift in Scotsman's cravat

indicators.note: in a down entry, taken over means placed above the next piece, so it comes first

parts.note: OW is a standard abbreviation for old woman
a relay is a shift of workers taking over from another

explanation.surface: An old lady has taken over a work shift wearing a Scotsman's cravat.
explanation.walkthrough: Owrelay is a Scots word, a form of overlay; Chambers marks it as Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots an owrelay is a cravat or neckcloth, literally something laid over the neck.

clue.text: Final exam one's working on in overcoat (7, two words)

indicators.note: in places the first idea inside the coat that follows, wrapping it

parts.note: a grego is a short hooded Levantine coat or overcoat
what you are working on is what you are at, as in 'what are you at?'

explanation.surface: Someone is studying for their final exam while still wearing an overcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: Grego is a rare word, a hooded Levantine coat. Great go is old Cambridge slang for the final BA examination, as opposed to the little go.
explanation.definitionFit: At Cambridge the great go was the final examination for the BA degree, as opposed to the little go.

clue.text: Mug for pet?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for the face
second meaning: a cat, a household pet

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a mug would suit their pet.
explanation.walkthrough: Mug reads as a cup, but it is slang for the face.
explanation.definitionFit: Puss is slang for the face (a mug) and a familiar name for a cat, the classic pet.

clue.text: Granny fed tart, requiring old-fashioned bib

indicators.note: something fed is taken inside, so the second word goes into the first

parts.note: nan is a familiar word for grandmother
tart and pro are both slang for a prostitute

explanation.surface: Grandma ate a tart and needed a bib.
explanation.walkthrough: Tart looks like pastry but is the slang for a prostitute.
explanation.definitionFit: Napron is the earlier form of apron (a napron became an apron), so it is an archaic word for a bib or pinafore.

clue.text: Whisper name, tense inside

indicators.note: inside says one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a title is a name, as of a book
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Whisper a name while feeling nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: Tense looks like an adjective about nerves but is the grammar term.
explanation.definitionFit: To tittle is a dialect verb meaning to whisper or tattle, as in tittle-tattle.

clue.text: Type of harp creating clash with a cor heartlessly played

indicators.note: played suggests notes performed in a new order, so the letters are rearranged
without its heart, the word loses its central letter

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, before losing its middle

explanation.surface: A harp and a French horn clash badly in a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: Cor is French for horn, which keeps the musical scene; losing its heart it gives CR.
explanation.definitionFit: The clarsach is the small traditional Celtic harp of Scotland and Ireland.

clue.text: Wind catching end of hair in part of Jock's beard

indicators.note: catching means holding something inside, so one piece goes in the other

parts.note: the bise is a cold north wind of Switzerland and southern France

indicators.note: end of picks out the final letter of the next word

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: The wind has caught the end of a Scotsman's beard.
explanation.walkthrough: Jock is a nickname for a Scotsman, signalling a Scots word; birse is Scots for a bristle.
explanation.definitionFit: Birse is Scots for bristle, and bristles make up a beard, so one is a part of it.

clue.text: Drudge had nothing on disposing of bundle outside

indicators.note: disposing of something means getting rid of it, so letters are removed
outside says the letters removed are those on the outer edges

parts.note: someone who had nothing on was naked
a wad is a bundle, as of banknotes

explanation.surface: A worn-out drudge was found with nothing on, having got rid of a bundle.
explanation.walkthrough: The bundle WAD is split: W and A come off the front of WAS NAKED, D off the end, leaving SNAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives snake as a dialect verb meaning to drudge or toil, so it matches drudge as a verb.

clue.text: Wanting readies I don't spread lavishly

indicators.note: spreading something lavishly scatters it everywhere, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: readies is slang for cash; the words are used for their letters

explanation.surface: A short-of-cash person protests that they do not throw their money about.
explanation.walkthrough: Readies is British slang for ready cash, which suits the surface about money.
explanation.definitionFit: Desideration is the state of desiring or lacking something, which is what wanting means as a noun.

clue.text: Reduced height pursued by planes, very fine

indicators.note: being pursued means something follows behind, so the next piece comes after

parts.note: height cut down to its abbreviation
an airline is a company operating planes

explanation.surface: Planes chase something flying at reduced height, in a near miss.
explanation.walkthrough: Reduced here means shortened to an abbreviation, not lowered.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairline crack or margin is extremely narrow, so as an adjective it means very fine.

clue.text: Salad garnish Escoffier's devised — not the off-licence!

indicators.note: something devised is newly put together, so the letters are rearranged
not signals that what follows is taken away

parts.note: the name with its possessive s
offie is British slang for an off-licence, a shop selling alcohol to take away

explanation.surface: The great chef Escoffier invented a salad garnish, not something from the liquor store.
explanation.walkthrough: Auguste Escoffier was a famous French chef, which keeps the scene culinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Cress is a peppery leafy plant commonly sprinkled over salads and sandwiches as a garnish.

clue.text: Fruit creation of banana with raspberries

indicators.note: the fruit is a creation made from the two words joined, keeping only the letters around the join and dropping the rest

parts.note: the first fruit, of which only the tail end is kept
the second fruit, of which only the opening is kept

explanation.surface: A dessert made from bananas and raspberries.
explanation.walkthrough: Azed asks you to run the two fruit words together; the answer straddles the join, the last two letters of one and first three of the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The naras is a spiny melon-like plant of south-west Africa whose edible fruit has the same name.

clue.text: A naker's not the first struck for old emperor

indicators.note: something struck is knocked about, so the letters are knocked into a new order
not the first means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a naker is an old kettledrum; the word with its possessive s

explanation.surface: A drum is struck to herald an old emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: A naker is a medieval kettledrum, so struck suits the surface as well as signalling the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Keasar is an obsolete spelling of kaiser, a word for an emperor.

clue.text: Against hazard I released fish

parts.note: to can mean against, as in back to back

indicators.note: released means let go, so that letter is let out of the word

parts.note: a hazard is a risk
the letter taken out

explanation.surface: Against the danger, I let the fish go.
explanation.definitionFit: The torsk is a North Atlantic food fish of the cod family, also called the tusk.

clue.text: Writer, English, gets wind up inside like a lot of old fossils

definitions.text: like a lot of old fossils

indicators.note: inside says this piece goes within the writer

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to wind is to coil
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: An English writer gets wound up, like plenty of old fogeys.
explanation.walkthrough: Old fossils in the surface suggests elderly people; it is meant literally, of fossils from a geological epoch.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliocene describes the geological epoch about 5 to 2.6 million years ago, the age of many fossils.

clue.text: Rape without passion, ecstasy, look, being limited

indicators.note: being limited means held within bounds, so these pieces are enclosed by another

parts.note: cold means unemotional
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
to look is to see

explanation.surface: A grim list of words about a cold, drug-fuelled act.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the plant: rape is oilseed rape, and coleseed is its seed or the plant itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleseed is the seed of cole, a brassica, and names the rape plant grown for oil.

clue.text: Sort of stew incorporating Latin slogan (7, two words)

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body, so the next piece goes inside

parts.note: a tagine is a North African slow-cooked stew
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A stew whose recipe comes with a Latin motto.
explanation.definitionFit: A tag line is a catchphrase or slogan used in advertising or attached to a brand.

clue.text: Shellfish tooth, bits in the wrong order

indicators.note: the two parts of the word swap places, the front chunk moving behind the back one

parts.note: a crena is a tooth or notch on a crenate edge, as of a leaf

explanation.surface: A shellfish's tooth whose parts have grown out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: Crena is a botanical word for a rounded tooth on a leaf edge; tooth seems to belong to the shellfish but is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives nacre as an old name for a shellfish yielding mother-of-pearl, as well as for the pearly lining itself.

clue.text: Flirts of old — they won't be singles

definitions.meaning: first meaning: people who chase the opposite sex, an older sense
second meaning: drinks taken after another, never on their own

explanation.walkthrough: Singles suggests unattached people, which flirts might be; here it means a single measure of spirits, and a chaser always follows another drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaser is both one who pursues romantically and a drink, often beer, taken after spirits.

clue.text: Backhand stroke fashioned by Rafa initially to a great extent

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the name before it

parts.note: its first letter
ever so means very much

explanation.surface: Rafa Nadal hits a stroke backhanded to great effect.
explanation.walkthrough: Rafa is the tennis player Rafael Nadal, which keeps the scene on court.
explanation.definitionFit: In real tennis a reverso is a backhand stroke, from Italian rovescio.

clue.text: Purulent result of botching DIY op

indicators.note: a botched job comes out jumbled, so the letters emerge in a new order

parts.note: used for its letters

explanation.surface: A do-it-yourself operation gone wrong leaves a festering wound.
explanation.walkthrough: DIY is do-it-yourself and op an operation, so the surface is a botched home surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: Pyoid means of the nature of pus, which is what purulent describes.

clue.text: Parent engaging chaplain as intermediary?

indicators.note: engaging means taking on or holding, so the next piece is held inside

parts.note: mater is Latin, and old schoolboy slang, for mother
CH is the abbreviation for chaplain

explanation.surface: A parent hires a chaplain to act as go-between.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: a matchmaker acts between two parties.
explanation.definitionFit: A matcher pairs people up, a matchmaker, who works as a go-between for a couple.

clue.text: Sad sack following one in a fog

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces within the next word

parts.note: mist is a fog
F is the abbreviation for following
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A hapless loser trails someone through the fog.
explanation.walkthrough: Sad sack is American slang for an inept, hapless person.
explanation.definitionFit: A misfit is someone who does not fit in, much like a sad sack, an inept or pitiable person.

clue.text: Jacques maybe going topless, about right get-up

indicators.note: about means around, so this piece goes round the next
in a down entry the top is the first letter, and going topless loses it

parts.note: Hattie Jacques was a British comic actress of the Carry On films
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A Frenchman named Jacques bares his top half while getting dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacques looks like a French first name, but it is a surname: Hattie Jacques, star of the Carry On comedy films; maybe marks her as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Get-up is informal for an outfit or costume, and attire is clothing.

clue.text: Turk requiring fragrant stuff, tiny amount applied

parts.note: otto, or attar, is a fragrant oil from rose petals
a mite is a very small amount

explanation.surface: A Turk wants some perfume, dabbing on just a little.
explanation.walkthrough: Otto of roses is the perfume oil also called attar.
explanation.definitionFit: Ottomite is an old word for an Ottoman, a Turk of the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Sojourn in vague W. European area of old? No thanks

indicators.note: no thanks says the word for thanks is absent, so those letters are taken away

parts.words: vague W. European area of old
parts.note: Tartary was an old, vaguely bounded name for lands of the Tatars
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: A traveller turns down an offer to stay in some vaguely defined old region.
explanation.walkthrough: Tartary had no fixed borders, hence vague; it ran from eastern Europe across Asia, so the W. in the clue is hard to square with it.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger or stay somewhere for a while, which is what sojourn means as a verb.

clue.text: Bunter was part of it, forgetting Latin in tests

indicators.note: forgetting something means leaving it out, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: trials are tests
L is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: Billy Bunter, the fat schoolboy of comic fiction, forgets his Latin in exams.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunter seems to be Billy Bunter of Greyfriars School stories; it is the Bunter sandstone, the lowest division of the Trias.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trias is the Triassic system of rocks, and the Bunter sandstone forms its lowest part.

clue.text: Corneal deposit? Philosopher has me accepting this

indicators.note: the philosopher's name is the first word accepting the answer inside it, so taking that word away leaves the answer

parts.note: Herbert Marcuse was a German-American philosopher
taken as written, split around this answer

explanation.surface: A philosopher claims to have a deposit on the eye.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the philosopher's name is made of ME holding the answer, which the clue calls this.
explanation.definitionFit: An arcus (arcus senilis) is a ring of fatty deposit around the cornea, common in old age.

clue.text: Piece of armour, something worth having after start of tilting

indicators.note: start of picks the first letter of the next word

parts.note: its first letter
an asset is something valuable

explanation.surface: Armour is a good thing to have when you start jousting.
explanation.walkthrough: Tilting is jousting on horseback, which keeps the armour scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A tasset is one of the plates hanging from the waist of a suit of armour to guard the thigh.

clue.text: What helps to render pugilist unconscious?

definitions.text: What helps to render pugilist unconscious?

indicators.note: what helps to make up a phrase is a part of it, so the answer is found inside the words

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A question about what knocks a boxer out.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue defines the answer, a blow that knocks a boxer out; read as wordplay, the answer helps to spell the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To stun is to knock someone senseless, which is how a boxer is rendered unconscious.

clue.text: Swallow maybe beginning to eat inside seed covering

indicators.note: inside says this letter sits within the seed covering

parts.note: an aril is a fleshy covering on some seeds

indicators.note: beginning to points to the first letter of the next word

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A swallow begins to eat inside a seed's coat.
explanation.walkthrough: Swallow looks like a verb next to eat; it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariel is the name of an Australian swallow, the fairy martin; maybe marks it as one example.

clue.text: Bellies formerly cauterized in part

indicators.note: in part means only a portion of the word is used, so the answer sits within it

parts.note: the letters inside this word

explanation.surface: Bellies were once partly cauterized in old surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: Formerly marks an obsolete sense: uterus once meant belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Uteri is the plural of uterus, which in older usage could mean the belly or abdomen.

clue.text: Strainer readjusted — it'll allow things to pass through

definitions.text: it'll allow things to pass through

indicators.note: readjusting changes the arrangement, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: used for its letters

explanation.surface: A sieve is adjusted to let things pass through it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like a strainer, but it is a customs document.
explanation.definitionFit: A transire is a customs warrant permitting goods to pass, so it lets cargo through.

clue.text: Boy trapping sea birds — does it help to support budget?

definitions.text: does it help to support budget?

indicators.note: trapping means holding something within, so the birds go inside

parts.note: a son is a boy
terns are sea birds

explanation.surface: A boy catches sea birds, perhaps to help the family finances.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: a sternson is a strengthening timber at a ship's stern.
explanation.definitionFit: A sternson is the end of a ship's keelson, a timber bracing the sternpost, so it supports the hull.
